summary.text: Take \(p=13\): the required quadratic-character conditions hold and \(13=3\cdot1^2+10\cdot1^2\); moreover, every integer representation \(13=3x^2+10y^2\) forces \(x^2=y^2=1\). Since \(\left(\frac{-1}{13}\right)=1\), the conjecture predicts \(S(13)\equiv 2\cdot13-12=14\pmod{169}\), whereas direct finite evaluation gives \(S(13)\equiv138\pmod{169}\).

full_proof.text:
We disprove the conjecture by taking the prime
\[
p=13.
\]
The failure occurs in clause (3).

Recall that the generalized central trinomial coefficient is
\[
T_k(b,c)=[X^k](X^2+bX+c)^k.
\]
To obtain a term of degree \(k\), choose \(i\) of the \(k\) factors to contribute \(X^2\), another \(i\) factors to contribute \(c\), and the remaining \(k-2i\) factors to contribute \(bX\). Therefore
\[
T_k(b,c)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}
 \binom{k}{i}\binom{k-i}{i}b^{k-2i}c^i.
\]
For a prime \(p\), the sum in the conjecture is
\[
S(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\binom{2k}{k}T_k(2,81)T_k(14,81).
\]

First we check all the hypotheses of clause (3) for \(p=13\). Clearly, \(13\) is prime and \(13>7\). The nonzero quadratic residues modulo \(13\) are
\[
1,3,4,9,10,12.
\]
Thus
\[
\left(\frac{3}{13}\right)=1,
\qquad
\left(\frac{2}{13}\right)=-1,
\qquad
\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)=-1.
\]
These are also compatible with the notation in the original clause, where the other two characters are written \((p/3)\) and \((p/5)\): indeed
\[
\left(\frac{13}{3}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)=1,
\qquad
\left(\frac{13}{5}\right)=\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)=-1.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
13=3\cdot 1^2+10\cdot 1^2,
\]
so \(13\) has the representation required in clause (3).

We now calculate \(S(13)\) modulo \(13^2=169\). Using the displayed finite formula for \(T_k(b,c)\), reduce the two generalized trinomial coefficients, the central binomial coefficient, and their product modulo \(169\). The complete calculation for \(0\leq k\leq12\) is as follows. Every entry in the four right-hand columns is a residue modulo \(169\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r|r}
k&\binom{2k}{k}&T_k(2,81)&T_k(14,81)&
\binom{2k}{k}T_k(2,81)T_k(14,81)\\ \hline
0&1&1&1&1\\
1&2&2&14&56\\
2&6&166&20&147\\
3&20&135&84&2\\
4&70&6&91&26\\
5&83&38&45&139\\
6&79&162&102&40\\
7&52&112&129&91\\
8&26&150&65&0\\
9&117&14&22&39\\
10&39&23&164&78\\
11&26&166&45&39\\
12&156&116&142&156
\end{array}
\]

For clarity, this table is obtained directly from
\[
T_k(b,81)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}
\binom{k}{i}\binom{k-i}{i}b^{k-2i}81^i
\]
with \(b=2\) and \(b=14\), followed by multiplication by \(\binom{2k}{k}\), always reducing modulo \(169\). Summing the last column gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(13)
&\equiv 1+56+147+2+26+139+40+91+0+39+78+39+156\\
&=814\\
&\equiv 138 \pmod{169},
\end{aligned}
\]
because \(814-4\cdot169=138\).

It remains to compare this with the value asserted by clause (3). Since \(13\equiv1\pmod4\), \(-1\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(13\); equivalently,
\[
\left(\frac{-1}{13}\right)=1.
\]
Taking the exhibited representation \(13=3\cdot1^2+10\cdot1^2\), clause (3) predicts
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(13)
&\equiv \left(\frac{-1}{13}\right)(2\cdot13-12\cdot1^2)\\
&=1\cdot(26-12)\\
&=14 \pmod{169}.
\end{aligned}
\]
But the actual value is \(138\pmod{169}\), and
\[
138-14=124
\]
is not divisible by \(169\). Hence the asserted congruence is false.

In fact, the contradiction does not depend on making an unfortunate choice among several representations. Suppose integers \(x,y\) satisfy
\[
13=3x^2+10y^2.
\]
Both terms on the right are nonnegative, so \(10y^2\leq13\), hence \(y^2\leq1\). If \(y=0\), then \(3x^2=13\), which is impossible. Therefore \(y^2=1\), and substituting back gives
\[
3x^2=13-10=3,
\]
so \(x^2=1\). Thus every integral representation of \(13\) by \(3x^2+10y^2\) yields exactly the same proposed residue
\[
\left(\frac{-1}{13}\right)(2\cdot13-12x^2)=14.
\]
None can yield the actual residue \(138\).

Consequently \(p=13\) satisfies every hypothesis of clause (3), including the required quadratic-form representation, but violates its conclusion modulo \(p^2\). Therefore Conjecture 3 for OEIS A336982 is false.
